ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Milwaukee, WI
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness surveys and weld inspection at Milwaukee plants, fab shops, boilers, piping and bridges. Technicians mobilized to site. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Milwaukee, Wisconsin
ut.html:
Atlantis performs ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection (UT) at Milwaukee plants, fabrication shops, terminals and utility sites. Typical scopes are wall-thickness surveys on process and steam piping, plate and vessel readings, and angle-beam examination of structural and pressure welds. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope. To start, send drawings, materials and access details through the UT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic inspection is used in Milwaukee

Milwaukee is a heavy-fabrication city. The Menomonee River Valley and the south-side industrial corridors hold foundries, forge shops, machine shops and plants that weld large frames for cranes, mining machinery, engines and power transmission equipment. Those welds see cyclic load, so owners and their customers often ask for volumetric examination of groove welds and thickness checks on plate before machining.

The second large group is utilities and buildings. District steam, hot-water heating and process boilers serve hospitals, universities, breweries and food plants across the metro area, and every one of them has piping and vessel walls that thin over time. UT readings at fixed locations show how fast that is happening. Port Milwaukee on Lake Michigan adds crane rails, cargo-handling structures and storage tanks at the harbor, and the city's many movable river bridges carry steel members and trunnion hardware that need periodic examination.

What UT finds in Milwaukee steel, and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing sends sound into the metal and reads the echoes. A straight-beam probe measures remaining wall by timing the back-wall echo. An angle-beam probe sends shear waves into a weld at 45, 60 or 70 degrees and reads reflections from lack of fusion, cracks and slag. Because the sound travels through the full thickness, UT sees buried flaws that surface methods cannot.

It also has limits that matter in a foundry city. Coarse-grained castings and some austenitic welds scatter sound and make interpretation unreliable, so a casting that looks fine to a straight beam may still need a different method or a modified procedure. Rough or scaled surfaces spoil coupling, tight geometry limits probe access, and a weld flaw lying parallel to the beam can be missed. A Level II chooses the probe and angle for the geometry, and the procedure states what the technique can and cannot detect.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Milwaukee UT work

Acceptance always comes from the construction or in-service code, not from the technician. For pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1, the ultrasonic weld requirements sit in Mandatory Appendix 12. Process piping under ASME B31.3 refers to the examination requirements in paragraph 344.6 and the criteria in Table 341.3.2. The examination method is written to ASME Section V: Article 4 for welds, Article 5 for materials, and the thickness measurement practice in Article 23 (SE-797).

Structural steel follows AWS D1.1, which has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds. Steel highway and railroad bridges follow AWS D1.5. Wisconsin regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Department of Safety and Professional Services under chapter SPS 341, and the City of Milwaukee Department of Neighborhood Services also keeps boiler inspectors and a boiler code in the city ordinances. For in-service equipment under OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), the owner must inspect to recognized good engineering practice, and thickness data is the usual evidence.

How a thickness survey is carried out

A Milwaukee thickness survey starts with the owner's drawing or isometric and a list of condition monitoring locations (CMLs). The technician calibrates the instrument on a step block of the same material, checks the zero, and takes readings at each CML on a marked grid so the next campaign can return to exactly the same spot. For corroded or pitted surfaces a dual-element probe is used, and the A-scan is watched rather than trusting a digital number alone, because doubling and pit echoes can make a thin wall read thick.

Hot lines are common in steam and process systems, so high-temperature probes and couplant are selected and readings are corrected for temperature. Coatings are either removed at the test spot or measured with a technique that is verified through the coating. The practice behind all of this is ASTM E797 and ASME Section V Article 5. See the national ultrasonic testing page and the guide to Article 5 thickness measurement for the general method.

How a weld examination is carried out

Weld examination begins with the procedure: joint design, thickness, scan plan, probe frequency and angle, couplant, and the reference level. The technician builds the reference from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, sets the scanning gain, and scans from both sides of the weld where access allows. Indications are located along the weld, across it and by depth, then evaluated against the acceptance table that the code names.

A Milwaukee fabricator welding thick plate for a crane boom or a gearbox housing will usually want the examination done after any required heat treatment and before final machining, because repairs are cheaper before the part is finished. Delayed cracking in heavy sections is one reason the examination timing is written into the procedure. ASTM E164 covers contact ultrasonic examination of weldments, and ASTM E114 covers straight-beam contact work on plate and forgings.

Who performs and reviews the work

Atlantis technicians are qualified under the company written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up and calibrates the equipment and performs and interprets the examination. Procedures are signed off by an ASNT Level III, who also reads the finished report before release. The company's Level III of record is the founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer issues certification to its own people, so the written practice you or your contractor operates under is the document that counts.

If a Milwaukee owner already has a written practice, we work to it and note any differences before mobilizing. If it needs updating, the written practice development service and Level III consulting are available separately.

What a Milwaukee UT report contains

  • Component or line identification, drawing reference and the material and nominal thickness.
  • The procedure number and revision, the code edition, and the acceptance criteria applied.
  • The instrument, probes, couplant and calibration block, with the calibration checks made during the job.
  • The technician's name and level, and the Level III who reviewed the report.
  • For thickness work, a grid or CML table with each reading, the previous reading if supplied, and the calculated loss.
  • For weld work, each indication's location, length, depth and amplitude, with accept or reject against the named table, and a sketch of the joint.

Readings that fall below the owner's minimum are flagged to your inspector at the time, not buried in the final document. Atlantis reports the data; decisions on repair, re-rating or continued service belong to the owner and the inspector responsible under the governing code.

Why Milwaukee walls thin: the mechanisms behind the readings

Knowing the damage mechanism tells the technician where to look. Steam condensate lines in the older district and building systems corrode from carbonic acid where condensate collects, so low points, traps and elbows get extra readings. Cooling-water and chilled-water piping thins from oxygen corrosion and from erosion at tight bends. Wisconsin road salt and lake-air moisture attack outdoor tanks, supports and bridge steel from the outside, especially where water pools under insulation or at the base of a column.

Process lines in brewing, food and chemical plants see cleaning chemicals and caustic washes, and thinning there is often localized at weld heat-affected zones and at the first elbow downstream of a pump. A thickness survey that follows these mechanisms, rather than a uniform grid, finds the worst locations sooner and gives the owner's inspector a more honest picture of remaining life. We ask owners for the operating history and the failure history so the CML list reflects it.

What a single thickness reading can and cannot tell you

A reading is one number at one spot. It is useful for trend, because the same CML read the same way each campaign shows a loss rate. It is poor evidence of an isolated pit that the probe did not happen to touch. For that reason surveys on suspect equipment often add a scan pattern around the CML rather than a single point, and the report flags any scatter between neighboring readings as a reason for closer work. Laminations in plate show up as an early back-wall echo and are recorded separately from corrosion.

Remaining life and next inspection dates are calculated by the owner's engineer or inspector from these readings under API 510, API 570 or API 653 where those codes apply. Atlantis supplies repeatable, well-documented data; the interval and the fitness decision are not ours to make. The ultrasonic testing guide covers the method in more depth.

Planning a UT job in Milwaukee

Lake Michigan winters set the planning calendar. Couplant thickens and can freeze on cold steel, instrument displays slow down in low temperatures, and outdoor work on tanks, bridges and rail structures is often limited to the milder months. Summer humidity brings condensation on cold lines. Plant outages in the metro area tend to cluster around spring and fall maintenance windows, so reserving capacity early for a shutdown scope is sensible.

Access matters as much as weather: scaffolding or lift access for elevated piping, insulation removal at test points, confined-space permits for vessels, and badging and safety orientation at industrial sites. Port terminals add their own security procedures. Give us the drawings, the last campaign's readings, operating temperatures and the permit rules, and the scope can be built around them.

UT, MT or PT for your Milwaukee job

Choose the method by the question. If you need wall thickness or a buried weld flaw, UT is the tool. If you need surface cracks in carbon or low-alloy steel, magnetic particle inspection in Milwaukee is faster and more sensitive at the surface. If the material is stainless steel, aluminum or another non-magnetic alloy and you are looking for surface-breaking cracks, liquid penetrant testing in Milwaukee is the match. Many jobs combine them: UT for the volume of a repair weld, then MT or PT on the finished surface.

Training your own UT technicians

Milwaukee shops that run their own inspection group can train through UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 courses, with theory delivered online and the practical completed with an ASNT Level III. The UT simulator lets trainees rehearse calibration and scanning before touching a real part. Local programs are listed on the NDT training in Milwaukee page.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic testing cost to quote for a Milwaukee site?
faq.a: Every job is scoped individually, so a quote follows from the drawings, materials, number of locations, access needs and the governing code. Send those through the quote form and we reply within one business day with what we need next.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on Milwaukee weld inspections?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 each contain ultrasonic provisions, and ASME Section VIII allows it only under specific conditions. The owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector must agree before the work starts.

faq.q: Does UT work on foundry castings in Milwaukee?
faq.a: It can for thickness checks and some flaw searches, but coarse grain scatters sound and limits reliability on many castings. The procedure should state the casting grade and the probes chosen, and a different method may be better for surface cracks.

faq.q: How do technicians handle hot piping during a UT thickness survey?
faq.a: They use high-temperature probes and couplant rated for the surface temperature, and correct the readings for the temperature effect on sound velocity. Very hot lines may need to be surveyed during a shutdown instead.

faq.q: Will you inspect bridge steel in Milwaukee?
faq.a: We can examine steel members and welds to the requirements the owner specifies, normally AWS D1.5 for bridge welds. Access, traffic control and permits are arranged by the owner or the prime contractor before technicians travel to the site.

faq.q: Who decides whether a thin reading is acceptable?
faq.a: The owner and the inspector responsible under the governing code decide. Under API 510, 570 or 653 that is the owner's authorized inspector. Atlantis performs the examination and reports the data, including readings below the stated minimum.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Milwaukee?
faq.a: No. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, with a Level II doing the work and an ASNT Level III reviewing procedures and reports. Travel and mobilization are planned with you when the scope is quoted.

faq.q: What information makes a Milwaukee UT scope quick to quote?
faq.a: Drawings or isometrics, material and nominal thickness, operating temperature, coating or insulation, the list of CMLs or weld joints, the governing code and edition, site access rules and the dates of any planned outage.

faq.q: Can Milwaukee technicians learn UT through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. Level 1 and Level 2 theory is delivered online, the practical is completed with an ASNT Level III, and employers issue the certification under their own written practice once experience hours are documented.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Milwaukee, WI | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection of welds, castings, forgings and structural steel at Milwaukee foundries, fab shops and plants. Mobilized to site. Get a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Milwaukee, Wisconsin
mt.html:
Atlantis performs magnetic particle inspection (MT) on ferromagnetic welds, castings, forgings and structural steel at Milwaukee foundries, fabrication shops, plants and port facilities. Technicians mobilize to your site, work to a written procedure, and report each indication against the acceptance criteria your code names. Send the component list, surface condition and access details through the MT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Milwaukee

Few American cities have as much heavy steel work packed into one metro area. Milwaukee's foundries pour gray iron, ductile iron and steel castings, its forge shops make shafts and gear blanks, and its fabricators weld frames, booms and housings for cranes, mining machines and drivelines. All of these are ferromagnetic, they carry cyclic loads, and the failure mode that worries owners is a fatigue crack that starts at a surface discontinuity. That is exactly what MT is built to find.

Outside the shops, MT is used on lifting lugs and pad eyes before heavy picks, on crane runway and hook details at the Lake Michigan harbor, on structural welds in buildings and bridges, and on repair excavations before rewelding. Brewery and food-plant jobs rarely need MT because their vessels are stainless steel, which is not magnetic, but the carbon steel supports, platforms and structural frames around them often do.

What MT finds, and what it misses

Magnetic particle testing magnetizes a ferromagnetic part and applies fine iron particles. Where a crack or seam interrupts the field, flux leaks out of the surface and the particles gather, drawing a visible line. It detects surface-breaking and slightly subsurface discontinuities such as cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts and incomplete fusion at the toe of a weld.

It works only on ferromagnetic material. Carbon and low-alloy steels and most cast irons qualify; austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys do not, and those go to penetrant testing instead. The field must cross the discontinuity at a useful angle, which is why two examinations at roughly right angles are required. MT does not size depth, does not find deep internal flaws, and thick paint or scale can weaken the indication. Residual magnetism after the test can also be a nuisance on machined parts.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Milwaukee MT work

The method is written to ASME Section V Article 7, which sets how the part is magnetized, the equipment checks, the lighting for visible particles and the ultraviolet intensity for fluorescent ones. ASTM E709 is the guide behind it and ASTM E1444 is the practice many specifications cite. For pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1, Mandatory Appendix 6 gives the MT method and its acceptance standards. Process piping under ASME B31.3 uses paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2.

Structural fabrication in Wisconsin usually follows AWS D1.1, and bridge members follow AWS D1.5, both of which accept MT as a surface examination. The owner of an in-service boiler or pressure vessel in Wisconsin deals with the Department of Safety and Professional Services under SPS 341, and repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code. The Article 7 explainer walks through the method requirements in plain language.

Technique: yokes, prods, wet and dry

For field work in Milwaukee the standard tool is the electromagnetic yoke. An AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and the technician proves this with a test weight before the shift. Prods pass current directly into the part and are used on heavy sections, but they can arc-burn the surface, so many procedures restrict them or forbid them on finished parts.

Visible dry powder suits rough welds and hot surfaces. Wet visible and wet fluorescent suspensions are more sensitive, and fluorescent work needs a darkened area and UV-A light at the intensity the procedure states. A field indicator, such as a pie gauge or shim, confirms that the field is strong enough in the direction needed. After the examination, parts that will be machined, welded or run near sensitive instruments are demagnetized and the residual field is checked.

Typical discontinuities in Milwaukee castings, forgings and weldments

Each product form fails in its own way, and the technician looks for it. Castings show shrinkage cracks, hot tears and cold shuts, often near section changes, and heavy gray and ductile iron parts can also show surface porosity that clusters into a visible indication. Forgings show laps, seams and quench or grinding cracks, usually running along the grain direction. Weldments show toe cracks, crater cracks, lack of sidewall fusion and underbead cracking in hardenable steels.

In service, fatigue cracks start at stress concentrations: fillet toes, keyways, the root of gear teeth, lifting-lug welds and weld terminations on crane structure. Those are the places a Milwaukee owner usually asks us to look. Arc strikes and grinding burns, which look minor, are also found and are recorded because they can start cracks later.

Heavy sections, coils and magnetizing current

Large Milwaukee parts such as crane hooks, shafts and thick-walled housings sometimes cannot be magnetized well with a handheld yoke. For those, a flexible cable wrapped around the part makes a coil that sets up a longitudinal field, and a central conductor threaded through a bore sets up a circular one. The procedure states the ampere-turns or current needed, and the part's length-to-diameter ratio influences how many shots are needed. Field indicators confirm the result on the actual surface.

Surface preparation, lighting and system checks

The result of an MT examination is only as good as the surface it is performed on. Heavy scale, loose paint, weld spatter and oil must be removed in the zone to be examined, and the surface should be dry. Under visible light, the part must be lit to the level the procedure states, measured with a light meter, and for fluorescent work the UV-A intensity at the surface and the ambient white light are both measured and recorded.

For wet systems the technician checks particle concentration with a settling test and confirms system performance on a reference part or ring. For dry systems the yoke lifting test is repeated whenever the equipment is moved or the pole spacing changes. These checks are what make a clean result believable, and they appear in the report so a reviewer can see they were done.

Who performs and reviews the work

A Level II technician qualified under the Atlantis written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets the indications. An ASNT Level III signs off the written procedure and checks the finished report before it leaves our hands. That review role is held by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, for Milwaukee magnetic particle work. The employer, not a training school, issues certification under SNT-TC-1A, so crews are expected to hold current records of training, experience, examination and vision checks.

Where a Milwaukee customer has its own procedure, we compare it with ASME Section V before mobilizing and raise any gaps in advance. A new or revised procedure can be prepared through Level III consulting.

What a Milwaukee MT report contains

  • The part, weld or casting identification, drawing reference, material and surface condition.
  • The procedure number and revision, the code and edition, and the acceptance standard used.
  • The method: yoke, prods, coil or other technique, wet or dry, visible or fluorescent, and the particle product.
  • Equipment checks: yoke lifting test, light meter readings, particle concentration and system performance.
  • Each indication's location, orientation and length, with a sketch or marked photograph and an accept or reject decision.
  • Demagnetization performed and the technician and reviewing Level III by name and level.

Relevant, non-relevant and false indications are separated in the record, because not every particle gathering is a defect. Atlantis reports what was found; disposition and repair belong to the owner under the governing code.

Planning an MT job in Milwaukee

Winter is the main constraint. Visible and fluorescent liquids behave differently on cold steel, condensation forms when cold parts are brought into a warm shop, and gloved hands make fine yoke placement harder. Procedures should state the lowest surface temperature the technique has been demonstrated at. In summer, hot sun on outdoor steel changes how carriers dry. Fluorescent work outdoors needs a tent or blackout cover so ambient light stays within the limit.

Foundry and forge schedules often drive timing: castings are examined after cleaning and before machining, forgings after heat treatment. Industrial sites require badging and orientation, and harbor facilities have their own security rules. Surface preparation is the hidden cost of any MT job, since heavy scale, paint or weld spatter has to come off at the examination zone.

Repair excavations and in-service checks

One of the most common reasons a Milwaukee owner calls for MT is a repair. When a crack is ground out of a weld or a casting, the excavation is examined by MT before welding to prove the crack is gone, and the finished repair is examined again after grinding. The same sequence applies to temporary attachments removed from vessels or structural steel. Recording both examinations in one report gives the owner and the inspector a clear chain of evidence.

MT, PT or UT for your Milwaukee job

If the part is carbon or low-alloy steel and the concern is a surface crack, MT is the quickest and most sensitive field choice. If it is stainless steel, aluminum or any non-magnetic alloy, use dye penetrant inspection in Milwaukee. If the question is wall thickness or a flaw buried inside a weld, use ultrasonic testing in Milwaukee. The national magnetic particle testing page covers the method in more depth, and the comparison guide MT versus PT helps when the material is borderline.

Training your own MT technicians

Employers with their own inspection staff can train people through MT Level 1 and MT Level 2, with online theory and a practical finished with an ASNT Level III. The NDT training in Milwaukee page lists the options, and the practice tests help candidates prepare for the written examinations.

faq.q: Which Milwaukee components can be inspected with magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Any ferromagnetic steel or iron part: welds on crane booms and frames, cast housings, forged shafts and gear blanks, lifting lugs, structural connections and repair excavations. Stainless steel and aluminum parts need penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: How do wet fluorescent and dry visible particles differ in Milwaukee field work?
faq.a: Wet fluorescent suspensions are more sensitive and need a darkened area and UV-A light, while dry visible powder is simpler in the field and works on rough or warm surfaces. The procedure chooses based on the code and the finish.

faq.q: Does MT find cracks under paint in Milwaukee?
faq.a: A thin, non-conductive coating of limited thickness may be tolerated if the technique is qualified for it, but heavy paint or scale weakens the indication. The procedure states the maximum coating thickness, and otherwise the coating is removed in the test zone.

faq.q: Why is MT done twice on the same weld?
faq.a: A crack is revealed only when the magnetic field crosses it at a useful angle, so ASME Section V requires two examinations at roughly right angles. That way cracks running in any direction are detected.

faq.q: Is demagnetization always required after MT?
faq.a: Not always. It is done when residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining, coating or service, or when the specification asks for it. The technician checks the residual field and records the result in the report.

faq.q: Can you perform MT on stainless steel brewery tanks in Milwaukee?
faq.a: Not with magnetic particles, because austenitic stainless steel is not ferromagnetic. Liquid penetrant testing is the correct surface method for stainless welds, and carbon steel supports around the tanks can still be examined by MT.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a lab or crew in Milwaukee?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in the city. Technicians travel to your plant, shop or yard for the agreed scope, and an ASNT Level III reviews the procedure and the report that comes out of it.

faq.q: What do you need from me to quote an MT job?
faq.a: Component or weld list, material, surface condition and coating, size and access, the governing code and edition, whether fluorescent or visible particles are required, dates, and any site safety or badging rules we must meet.

faq.q: How quickly will an MT crew start work in Milwaukee?
faq.a: Start dates depend on scope, permits and travel arrangements, which we confirm when the job is quoted. We do not promise an arrival time before the scope, site access and procedure are agreed with you.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Milwaukee, WI | Liquid PT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection of stainless, aluminum and carbon steel welds at Milwaukee breweries, plants and shops. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Milwaukee, Wisconsin
pt.html:
Atlantis performs liquid penetrant testing (PT), also called dye penetrant inspection, on welds, castings and machined parts at Milwaukee breweries, food and beverage plants, fabrication shops and industrial sites. PT finds surface-breaking cracks and porosity on stainless steel, aluminum and other non-porous metals. Technicians travel to your site. Send the material, finish and code through the PT quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Milwaukee

Milwaukee is a brewing and food-processing city, and those industries run on stainless steel: fermenters, kettles, heat exchangers, sanitary tubing, pumps and fittings. Stainless is not magnetic, so the standard surface examination for its welds is penetrant testing. Welds on tank nozzles, jacket attachments and sanitary tube joints are examined for cracks and pinholes that could harbor contamination or leak under pressure.

The same method fits the city's metalworking base. Aluminum weldments, non-ferrous castings, machined housings, and stainless or nickel-alloy components built for chemical, power and marine applications all pass through shops here. In the field, PT is used on repair excavations before rewelding, on socket and branch welds of small piping, and on the finished surface after grinding. It can also be used on carbon steel when MT is impractical, for example on a small fillet that a yoke cannot reach.

What PT finds, and what it misses

Penetrant testing relies on capillary action. A low-viscosity liquid is applied to a clean surface, enters any opening that reaches the surface, and after the excess is removed a developer draws it back out to form a visible indication. Cracks, laps, seams, porosity and incomplete fusion that break the surface show up clearly, with the color or fluorescence of the dye.

PT is blind to anything that does not open to the surface. A subsurface void, an internal lack of fusion or a crack closed by machining smear or peening will not show. Rough surfaces hold penetrant and create background, and parts that were blasted, ground or machined hard may have the openings smeared shut. Porous materials such as some castings or powder metal cannot be tested conventionally. Cleanliness drives everything: oil, paint, rust and weld flux must be removed first.

Codes, materials and acceptance criteria

The governing practice is ASME Section V Article 6, supported by ASTM E165 for general industry. For pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1, Mandatory Appendix 8 gives the penetrant method and acceptance standards, and process piping under ASME B31.3 uses paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2. Structural stainless fabrication under AWS D1.6 and carbon steel under AWS D1.1 accept PT as a surface check where the contract calls for it.

Material control matters on the alloys common in Milwaukee. Article 6 limits sulfur and halogen content in penetrant materials used on nickel-base alloys, austenitic stainless steel and titanium, because residues can cause damage in service. The technician records the batch numbers of cleaner, penetrant and developer so the limits can be demonstrated. Read the explainer on Article 6 liquid penetrant requirements for the method detail. Repairs to Wisconsin boilers and pressure vessels follow the National Board Inspection Code, with the state program run through the Department of Safety and Professional Services.

Technique: from precleaning to inspection

A penetrant examination has fixed steps and the procedure fixes the times. The surface is cleaned and dried, penetrant is applied by spray or brush, and it is allowed to dwell for the time the procedure states. Excess penetrant is removed by solvent wipe, water wash or an emulsifier depending on the system, a developer is applied thinly and evenly, and the surface is examined after the development time.

Type I systems are fluorescent and examined under UV-A light in a darkened area; Type II systems are visible dye and viewed in white light. Method A is water-washable, Method C is solvent-removable and is the usual field choice because it needs no water supply. Light levels at the part must meet the Article 6 limits. Final cleaning removes developer and penetrant residue, which brewery and food customers often require before a vessel returns to service.

Common ways penetrant jobs go wrong

Most poor PT results trace back to preparation, not the penetrant. Grinding, blasting or wire-brushing can smear metal over the very cracks being sought, which is why etching or careful mechanical cleaning is specified on machined and ground parts. Leftover oil, paint or rust blocks entry, and over-application of developer can mask small indications. Overly aggressive washing removes penetrant out of real cracks and gives a false clean result.

Timing mistakes are the next group. A dwell that is too short may not let penetrant reach tight cracks, and developer left too long can bleed and blur. Temperature outside the qualified range changes viscosity and evaporation. The procedure sets every one of these controls, and the technician records them so the owner can check that the process was followed as written.

Reading indications: relevant, non-relevant and false

Seeing a mark is not the same as having a defect. A relevant indication is caused by a discontinuity and is evaluated against the acceptance table. A non-relevant indication comes from a feature of the part, such as a sharp thread, a keyway, a press fit or a rough machined edge, and is recorded but not judged as a flaw. A false indication comes from handling or poor technique, such as penetrant left on a finger or a poorly washed surface.

Distinguishing these takes experience and a consistent procedure. When an indication is unclear, the technician wipes it away, reapplies developer and watches whether it returns in the same place and shape, which usually settles the question. Rounded and linear indications are measured and judged separately because acceptance tables treat them differently, and small indications below a stated size may be ignored by the code. The report records which rule was used so a reviewer can check the call.

Sanitary and food-grade considerations

Milwaukee's food and beverage plants set a higher bar than most industrial sites for what may touch a product-contact surface. Penetrant materials, solvents and developers are reviewed by the plant's quality team before use, and a post-examination cleaning step removes residues to the plant's standard. Weld finish on sanitary tubing is usually polished, which can close small cracks, so examination happens at the stage that gives a fair chance of an honest result.

Plants also keep records for their own audits, so the Atlantis report includes material batch information, the cleaning performed and the procedure revision. If a procedure for sanitary welds does not exist yet, Level III consulting can write one that suits the plant's quality system.

Who performs and reviews the work

PT is performed and interpreted by a Level II technician qualified under the Atlantis written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure, covering dwell times, temperature and material controls, and then reviews the report. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, fills that role for penetrant work in Milwaukee. Technicians must pass a near-vision check and a color-contrast check under the written practice, since reading faint indications is the whole job.

Customers who need a PT procedure for a new vessel or a food-grade repair program can request one through Level III consulting or written practice development.

What a Milwaukee PT report contains

  • The component, weld or part identification, material and surface finish, and the area examined.
  • Procedure number and revision, the code edition in force and the acceptance table used to judge each indication.
  • The penetrant type, method, sensitivity level and manufacturer, with batch numbers for cleaner, penetrant and developer.
  • Surface and material temperature, dwell and development times, and light measurements.
  • Each indication with location, size, shape and whether it is rounded or linear, plus an accept or reject decision.
  • Post-cleaning performed, and the technician and reviewing Level III by name and level.

Where the specification sets a threshold, such as treating small rounded indications as non-relevant, the report states which rule was applied. Atlantis records the evidence; disposition and repair decisions remain with the owner.

Planning a PT job in Milwaukee

The standard technique in ASME Section V Article 6 covers 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for both the part and the materials. A Milwaukee winter puts outdoor steel well below that range, and a sunny day on a rooftop or harbor structure can exceed it. Work below 40 degrees needs a qualified technique, or the part is warmed and sheltered. Cold penetrant also thickens and dwell times change, so the procedure should be demonstrated at the temperature actually expected.

Brewery and food-plant work is scheduled around production, with cleaning chemicals approved by the plant's quality team before they touch product-contact surfaces. Industrial sites require safety orientation and hot-work coordination. Surface preparation, especially removing coatings, labels or heat tint from stainless, should be built into the scope and schedule rather than discovered on the day.

Weld repairs and tube-to-tubesheet joints

Penetrant testing is also the usual check on small, awkward welds where other surface methods cannot reach, such as tube-to-tubesheet joints in heat exchangers, socket welds and instrument connections. Milwaukee plants with process heat exchangers use it after retubing or seal-weld repairs. As with any repair, the excavation is examined before welding and the finished weld afterward, and the report ties the two together for the owner's inspector.

PT, MT or UT for your Milwaukee job

Choose PT when the material is non-magnetic, the surface is machined or finished, or you need to see small surface-breaking flaws on stainless or aluminum. Choose magnetic particle testing in Milwaukee for carbon steel, where it also finds slightly subsurface flaws and tolerates a rougher surface. Choose ultrasonic testing in Milwaukee when the concern is wall loss or a flaw inside the weld. The national penetrant testing page has more on the method, and the MT versus PT guide helps when both could work.

Training your own PT technicians

PT is one of the quickest methods to learn well, and many Milwaukee employers start new inspectors here. PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 use online theory with a practical completed with an ASNT Level III, and the PT simulator gives trainees repetitions on dwell, removal and interpretation. See the Milwaukee NDT training page for the full list.

faq.q: What can liquid penetrant testing find on Milwaukee stainless steel tanks?
faq.a: Surface-breaking cracks, pinholes, porosity and incomplete fusion in welds, nozzles and jacket attachments. It cannot detect flaws that stay below the surface, so internal conditions need a different method such as ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: Are dye penetrant inspection and liquid penetrant testing one method?
faq.a: Yes. Dye penetrant inspection and liquid penetrant testing describe the same method. Visible dye penetrant is viewed in white light, while fluorescent penetrant is viewed under UV-A light in a darkened area.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to PT in Milwaukee winters?
faq.a: The standard technique in ASME Section V Article 6 covers 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature, or the part must be warmed or sheltered.

faq.q: Can PT be used on carbon steel as well as stainless steel?
faq.a: Yes. PT works on any clean, non-porous metal, ferrous or not. On carbon steel, magnetic particle testing is often preferred because it also finds slightly subsurface flaws, but PT is useful where a yoke cannot reach.

faq.q: Why are penetrant batch numbers recorded?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 limits sulfur and halogen content in materials used on nickel-base alloys, austenitic stainless steel and titanium. Recording batch numbers lets the owner demonstrate that compliant materials were used.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office or lab in Milwaukee?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Milwaukee. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, shop or yard for the agreed scope, working under a procedure approved by an ASNT Level III.

faq.q: Can you work around production at a Milwaukee brewery or food plant?
faq.a: Scheduling is planned with the plant: cleaning chemicals are approved in advance, product-contact surfaces are protected, and post-cleaning removes developer and penetrant residue. Specific shutdown dates are agreed when the scope is quoted.

faq.q: What do you need to quote a PT job?
faq.a: A list of welds or parts, material and finish, coating or heat tint to be removed, the code and edition, whether fluorescent or visible penetrant is required, temperature conditions, access and site safety requirements.

faq.q: Who issues PT personnel certification for my inspectors?
faq.a: Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer issues certification under its own written practice. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 and Level 2 training that supports that process, and the employer decides when its people are certified.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing (RT) Alternatives in Milwaukee, WI
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. Milwaukee options: UT, ASNT Level III review of radiographs, and RT training theory. Request a quote.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Alternatives in Milwaukee, Wisconsin
rt.html:
Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, and that applies in Milwaukee as everywhere else. US industrial radiography is a licensed activity: the radioactive sources and X-ray equipment involved are regulated under Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules in 10 CFR Part 34, or the equivalent rules of the state where the work is done. It is not a service Atlantis offers in Milwaukee or anywhere else in the country. This page explains what is available to a Milwaukee owner whose specification or search brought them to radiography.

Why Milwaukee owners ask for radiography

Milwaukee's welded pressure vessels, process piping, structural weldments and castings are often specified with radiographic examination, because a film or image shows volumetric flaws as a permanent record. Foundry buyers also grade castings against reference radiographs. When a project calls for RT, the owner hires a licensed radiography contractor. Atlantis does not recommend or name one, and the arrangement is between you and that contractor.

Ultrasonic testing as the volumetric alternative

Where the construction code and the owner allow it, ultrasonic testing can examine the full thickness of a weld without a radiation source. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, and AWS D1.1 has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds. ASME Section VIII permits ultrasonic examination to stand in for radiography under limited conditions only. Any substitution has to be agreed with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job. See ultrasonic testing in Milwaukee for how that work is done.

ASNT Level III radiography services that need no radiation licence

The review side of radiography needs no source and no exposure. An ASNT Level III can review radiographs, whether film or digital images, and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. That includes a second read on disputed indications, an independent look at image quality and coverage, and a review of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice before work starts. The reviewer is the founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and none of the review work involves a source or an exposure. Level III consulting and written practice development describe how engagements are set up.

Learning radiographic testing

Employers building their own radiography group can train technicians in theory through the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Theory is separate from the licensed hands-on exposure work, which a technician carries out under the licence of the employer or contractor. The NDT training in Milwaukee page lists the options available to local candidates, and the MT and PT pages cover the surface methods Atlantis does perform in the city.

How to get started

If you need UT, MT or PT in Milwaukee, or a Level III review of someone else's radiographs, send the specification and what you need examined through the quote form. Atlantis has no office in Milwaukee, so technicians are mobilized to your site for any on-site scope, and review work can often be done from the records alone. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can Atlantis do radiography in Milwaukee?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography is a licensed activity under NRC or state rules. Ultrasonic, magnetic particle and penetrant inspection and Level III review services are available instead.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace RT on a Milwaukee weld?
faq.a: Only where the code and the owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 have ultrasonic provisions, and ASME Section VIII allows it under specific conditions. Agree the substitution with the owner, engineer and inspector first.

faq.q: Can an ASNT Level III review radiographs taken by another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. A Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, give a second read on disputed indications and review the contractor's procedure and written practice.

faq.q: Does Atlantis train technicians in radiographic testing?
faq.a: Radiographic testing Level 2 theory training is available through Atlantis. The licensed hands-on exposure work is carried out under the licence of the employer or contractor, and the employer issues certification under its own written practice.

faq.q: Who should I contact for radiography in Milwaukee?
faq.a: A licensed radiography contractor holds the authority to do the work. Atlantis does not recommend or name one. Send us the specification if you want help with the review, ultrasonic alternatives or procedure checks.
